implementation_notes: The bulkhead is a limiter object per dependency: in Polly v8 the v7 Bulkhead policy became the rate limiter strategy, and AddConcurrencyLimiter(permitLimit, queueLimit) wraps each dependency call with a bounded slot count and an optional queue, rejecting with RateLimiterRejectedException when both are full; the same effect without Polly is System.Threading.RateLimiting.ConcurrencyLimiter (PermitLimit, QueueLimit, QueueProcessingOrder) obtained through a lease that must be disposed. Use this form when dependency calls are already asynchronous; the bounded-channel variant is for blocking calls that need dedicated consumers.

variants.name: Polly v8 concurrency limiter
variants.implementation_notes: The bulkhead is a limiter object per dependency: in Polly v8 the v7 Bulkhead policy became the rate limiter strategy, and AddConcurrencyLimiter(permitLimit, queueLimit) wraps each dependency call with a bounded slot count and an optional queue, rejecting with RateLimiterRejectedException when both are full; the same effect without Polly is System.Threading.RateLimiting.ConcurrencyLimiter (PermitLimit, QueueLimit, QueueProcessingOrder) obtained through a lease that must be disposed. Use this form when dependency calls are already asynchronous; the bounded-channel variant is for blocking calls that need dedicated consumers.
pitfalls: The Polly v7 Bulkhead policy is gone in v8; new code must use the rate limiter strategy (AddConcurrencyLimiter), not Policy.Bulkhead.
Sharing one limiter instance across unrelated dependencies recreates the coupling; each dependency or tenant needs its own limiter.
QueueLimit and QueueProcessingOrder decide whether new or old requests wait; after the queue fills the limiter rejects, so the pair is the real capacity policy.
A concurrency limiter does not bound call duration: a hung call holds its permit forever unless a timeout strategy is layered around it.

variants.name: Bounded channel with dedicated consumer tasks (worker isolation)
variants.implementation_notes: Worker-isolation variant: one bounded Channel<T> per dependency with N long-running consumer tasks; producers use TryWrite and treat a full channel as the saturation signal, so blocking dependency calls execute only on that dependency's dedicated tasks or dedicated TaskScheduler. This is the analogue of a thread-pool bulkhead and the right choice when the call is synchronous or blocking; the limiter variant is simpler when calls are already async.
pitfalls: Consumers started with Task.Run still run on the shared thread pool; use LongRunning tasks or a dedicated scheduler when the dependency call blocks.
BoundedChannelFullMode.Wait makes TryWrite fail immediately - choose Wait or DropWrite deliberately and make callers handle the false return.
Complete the channel on shutdown or consumer tasks keep waiting and can hang graceful termination.
A channel bounds pending work but not in-flight consumers; 8 consumers plus 16 queued is the real limit only if both are bounded.
